mem.t: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

lessons.title: A Change of Mindset
lessons.theme: Looking back over twelve weeks at how God has renewed my mind

v: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit,
and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind,
and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.

lessons.still: Find a quiet place and give yourself a little more time than usual. Open your notes from these twelve weeks, or simply recall the road you have traveled. Don’t rush to evaluate; just quietly say to the Lord, “Lord, take me back to see the footprints you have walked with me.”
teach: Climbers halfway up a mountain will sit down on a big rock and look back. Looking up, the summit is still far away; looking down, they discover how far they have already come. A retreat week is that rock. Stopping is not laziness; it is a chance to see clearly where we have come from, sort out our gear, and then keep climbing.

Paul describes sanctification in three movements: “put away” the old self, “be renewed in the spirit of your mind,” and “put on” the new self. The middle step is the key—renewal of the mind is a change of mindset. Over these twelve weeks we have experienced a whole series of shifts in perspective: from performance to grace (coming home), from busyness to stillness, from piling up knowledge to meeting God (reading Scripture), from my kingdom to your kingdom (prayer), from grasping power to returning to our place (humility and victory).

And more: from anxiety to rest, from feelings to assurance, from speed-reading to meditation, from complaint to thanksgiving, from living from the head by ourselves to living from the heart by the Spirit, from living for ourselves to living for others. Change your mindset and you change your life. Today, pick out the shift that has gone deepest for you and write: “I used to think…, but now I know….”
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps of changing our mindset—Information, Revelation, Conviction, Practice, Review, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. A retreat is the time for “Review” and “Correction.” Shifting from a human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, is a lifelong lesson—and we have already begun.
q: Who is God? — Looking back over twelve weeks, how has God renewed your mindset?
Who am I? — Which old way of thinking is the most stubborn, still tugging at you today?
How shall I respond? — Which new way of thinking will you carry into the next stage?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus walked with two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and “beginning from Moses and from all the prophets, he explained to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27). Their understanding was renewed by the Lord, their hearts burned within them, and they got up at once to return to Jerusalem. Jesus is glad to walk with us as we look back, helping us understand afresh the road we have traveled.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for walking with me these twelve weeks. You have renewed so many of my mistaken ideas and shown me your grace and truth. Keep renewing me in the spirit of my mind, so that I put off the old self and put on the new self, created in your likeness. I want to be renewed by you all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write three sentences beginning “I used to think…, but now I know…”
Review the memory verses from the past twelve weeks and see how many you still remember
Tell a spiritual companion about the deepest change of mindset you have experienced
lessons.noon: “And that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind” — Lord, right now keep renewing my heart.

lessons.title: A Change of Life
lessons.theme: When we remain in the Lord, our lives change naturally and bear fruit

v: Remain in me, and I in you. As the branch can’t bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.
I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.

lessons.still: Clench both hands into fists, a picture of gripping tightly in your own strength. Then slowly relax them and turn your palms upward, a picture of a branch simply joined to the vine. Quietly meditate on this week’s verse: “I am the vine. You are the branches.”
teach: A photograph captures a single moment, but growth only shows up in time-lapse. Looking at yourself day by day, nothing seems to change. But set yourself from twelve weeks ago beside yourself today, and you may notice: a little less temper, a little more prayer, a little more patience with your family.

Jesus says the branch’s secret to bearing fruit is just one thing: “Remain in me.” Not straining to squeeze out fruit, but staying connected. Paul also says that as we see “the glory of the Lord,” we “are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.” Change comes by beholding, not by striving. And it comes “from the Lord, the Spirit”: life change is the work of the Holy Spirit; our part is to remain in the Lord and fix our eyes on him.

So when you look back on how your life has changed, don’t only ask whether you have done well. Ask instead: over these twelve weeks, has my connection with the Lord grown closer? Stillness, Scripture, prayer, meditation, worship—these practices are not the fruit itself; they are the ways a branch stays joined to the vine. Get the connection right, and the fruit will come naturally.
lessons.light: 321 Light: “Apart from me you can do nothing”—this is the declaration of the self-emptied life. The self-ruled person tries to bear fruit by his own effort and grows ever drier; the self-emptied person remains in the Lord, lets Christ live within, and enters the limitless. Change your mindset and you change your life; change your life and you change your lifestyle.
q: Who is God? — What does the picture of the vine and the branches show you about God’s relationship with you?
Who am I? — Compared with twelve weeks ago, where do you see change in your life?
How shall I respond? — In the next stage, which practice will you use to keep “remaining in the Lord”?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works” (John 14:10). All his life he bore fruit in connection with the Father. He wants us to remain in him, just as he remains in the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and I am a branch. Thank you for the changes you have made in me over these twelve weeks—small, but real. Apart from you I can do nothing. Help me remain in you, fix my eyes on your glory, and be transformed by you from glory to glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write down three changes you have seen in your life over these twelve weeks
Ask a family member or friend, “Have you noticed anything different about me these past three months?”
lessons.noon: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.” — Lord, right now I remain in you.

lessons.title: Setting Up a Stone: A Record of Grace
lessons.theme: Counting God’s graces and raising an Ebenezer to his faithfulness

v: Then Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen, and called its name Ebenezer, saying, “The LORD helped us until now.”
It is because of the LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.

lessons.still: Quietly recall one specific way God helped you during these twelve weeks—an answered prayer, a timely comfort, a restored relationship. Treat it like a stone and gently set it down in your heart, saying, “Until now you have helped me.”
teach: Many families mark their children’s height on a doorframe, one line each year. When the children grow up and look back at those lines, they see the story of how they were raised. Our spiritual lives need “height marks” too—recording God’s grace so that in hard times we don’t forget how he once led us.

At Mizpah the Israelites repented and returned to God. When the Philistines came to attack, God thundered with a great voice and threw the enemy into confusion. Samuel then set up a stone and named it “Ebenezer,” meaning “stone of help,” saying, “Yahweh helped us until now.” This stone was both a look back (until now) and an act of faith (God will keep on helping). Jeremiah, too, amid the ruins of the city, remembered that God’s loving kindnesses “are new every morning.”

A record of grace is not boasting about our achievements; it is a testimony to God’s faithfulness. Today, write a list of the graces of these twelve weeks: prayers answered, mindsets renewed, relationships restored, days kept safe. This list will become fuel for the next stretch of the journey, and material for sharing your testimony with others in the future.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The final stop on the path of service is “God”—giving glory to God and giving thanks in everything. A record of grace helps us see that everything has been accomplished by God in Jesus, so the glory does not go to me but to Jesus. Counting God’s graces is a concrete way of letting Jesus receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — “They are new every morning.” How have you experienced God’s faithfulness these twelve weeks?
Who am I? — Do you tend to remember grace, or to forget it?
How shall I respond? — What kind of “Ebenezer” will you set up for these twelve weeks?
lessons.jesus: When Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper, he said, “Do this in memory of me” (Luke 22:19). He knew how forgetful we are, so he gave us a sign we could repeat again and again. Every time we take Communion, we set up another Ebenezer beneath the cross.
lessons.pray: Faithful Lord, until now you have helped me. Thank you for the new mercies of every morning these twelve weeks, for holding me up when I was weak and finding me when I was lost. I will remember your deeds and not forget your benefits. May this record be the beginning of a lifelong testimony to your faithfulness. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write a list of at least ten graces from these twelve weeks
Find a small stone or a card and write on it “Ebenezer” and today’s date
Share one grace from your list with a spiritual companion
lessons.noon: “The LORD helped us until now.” — Lord, right now I remember your faithfulness.

lessons.title: Stage Self-Review
lessons.theme: Examining ourselves honestly before the Lord to see the next step clearly

v: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith. Test your own selves. Or don’t you know about your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you?— unless indeed you are disqualified.

lessons.still: Before you begin the self-review, be still for a minute. Tell the Lord, “I am not doing this to give myself a score, or to condemn myself. I only want to see myself clearly in your light.” Let your heart settle, then answer honestly.
teach: After a certain number of miles, a car goes back to the garage for a service: the tyres are checked, the oil is changed, the steering is realigned. This is not because the car is broken but so that it can go further. The spiritual health self-review is the same—not an exam, but regular maintenance to see what has worn down and what needs adjusting.

David prayed, “Search me, God, and know my heart.” The best self-review is not looking in a mirror ourselves but asking God to shine his light, because the human heart is deceitful above all things and we need his light. Paul also urges believers to “examine your own selves” and “test your own selves,” and the focus of that examination is: “Don’t you know… that Jesus Christ is in you?” The heart of the self-review is not a grade but our relationship with Christ.

Face each question honestly: stillness, Scripture, prayer, humility, rest, meditation, worship, following the Spirit, self-denial—which have taken root, and which are still shallow? If your score is high, don’t be proud; if it is low, don’t be discouraged. Once you see clearly, choose one or two areas you most need and carry them into the next stage. This is “Review” and “Correction,” followed by “Repetition.”
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is the key to revival. The proud don’t want to be searched, afraid of seeing their shortcomings; the humble are willing to return to their place, letting God be God and people be people—admitting they need to grow. The purpose of the self-review is to let Jesus reign in more areas of our lives.
q: Who is God? — When God searches us, is it to condemn us, or to “lead me in the everlasting way”?
Who am I? — Among these practices, which is your strongest? Which is your weakest?
How shall I respond? — In the next stage, which one or two practices will you prioritize strengthening?
lessons.jesus: The risen Jesus asked Peter three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17). This was the gentlest and also the deepest examination. The Lord was not trying to humiliate him but to restore him. When we review ourselves before the Lord, the core question he asks is always the same: Do you love me?
lessons.pray: God, search me and know my heart; try me and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way. I am not afraid to be honest before you, because you are the Father who loves me. Show me where I need to grow stronger in the next step. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Complete this stage's spiritual health self-review
From the results of your self-review, circle the one practice that most needs strengthening
Share your self-review results with a spiritual parent or companion and ask them to pray for you
lessons.noon: “Search me, God, and know my heart.” — Lord, right now I open myself in your light.

lessons.title: Resolving to Enter Growing
lessons.theme: Deep roots make tall growth; forgetting what is behind, stretching forward to what is ahead

v: As therefore you received Christ Jesus the Lord, walk in him,
rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, even as you were taught, abounding in it in thanksgiving.
Brothers, I don’t regard myself as yet having taken hold, but one thing I do: forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.

lessons.still: Quietly stand up (or stand up in your heart) and face forward. Say to the Lord, “Lord, I have begun to put down roots; now I want to move forward with you.” Take one area in which you want to grow and receive it from the Lord’s hand, like a runner taking the baton.
teach: Some kinds of bamboo show little sign of life above ground for the first few years after planting, because they are spreading their roots underground. Once the roots are established, the speed of their upward growth is astonishing. These thirteen weeks of “Rooting” may not have been dramatic, but they have laid the foundation for the “Growing” to come.

Paul uses two pictures for Christian growth. First, “rooted and built up in him”—like a tree putting down roots, like a house laid on its foundation. Then, “forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal”—like a race. We put down roots in order to run, and we run by drawing on our roots. “Forgetting what is behind” means neither being bound by past failures nor resting on past achievements; “stretching forward” aims at “the prize of the high calling of God.”

This brings Stage One, “Rooting,” to a close. We came home; we learned stillness, Scripture reading, prayer, humility, victory and rest; we gained assurance; we learned meditation, worship, dependence on the Spirit and self-denial. In the next stage, “Growing,” we will set out from our identity in Christ and let branches and leaves grow from these roots. Write down one sentence of resolve, and with a thankful heart, press on toward the goal.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. Stage One put down roots in our relationship with God; the growth ahead will extend this life to ourselves, to others and to our tasks. Our one purpose: to build what belongs to God. We do not grow for our own sake, but so that Jesus may reign and receive all the glory.
q: Who is God? — The God who calls you “from above”—what are his intentions for your next stage?
Who am I? — What lies behind you that you need to “forget”—the chains of failure, or past achievements?
How shall I respond? — Write one sentence of resolve as you enter the “Growing” stage.
lessons.jesus: Scripture records that “Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men” (Luke 2:52). He spent many ordinary years in Nazareth before stepping out into public ministry. His growth was whole and steady; and today he lives in us, leading us step by step to grow up into maturity.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for bringing me through these thirteen weeks of rooting. I will forget what is behind, stretch forward to what is ahead, and press on toward the goal. Make me rooted and built up in you, established in the faith, and abounding in thanksgiving. Lead me into the season of growing; may you reign, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen.
acts: Write a sentence of resolve and put it up where you have your daily devotions
Choose two practices to continue in the next stage, and set a regular time for each
Invite a spiritual companion to commit with you to praying for each other through the next stage
lessons.noon: “Forgetting the things which are behind and stretching forward to the things which are before” — Lord, right now I move forward with you.
